steps.question: A video player adds the same number to a million pixels. Why not add 8 or 16 pixels per instruction? And why does a 1978 instruction set still run on your laptop?
clues: **Vector / SIMD** instructions apply one operation to many data items at once.
**RISC** designs keep instructions simple; **x86** kept compatibility for 45 years.
Today we also pull the whole course together.

steps.title: Scalar vs vector

head: Scalar
Vector / SIMD
rows: Many data items at once (a vector)
Wide registers holding several values (128, 256, 512 bits) or many elements

steps.why: When the same operation is applied to lots of data, one instruction can do the work of many, saving fetch, decode and energy.
steps.real: x86 has SSE and AVX; ARM has NEON and SVE; RISC-V has a vector extension; GPUs are massive SIMD machines.

explainAgain.beginner: A cashier scanning items one by one (scalar) versus a machine that scans a whole tray at once (vector).

steps.title: Try it: lanes and cycles
steps.why: 8 additions: 8 cycles with 1 lane, 4 with 2 lanes, 2 with 4 lanes and 1 with 8 lanes. The speed-up equals the number of lanes when the work divides evenly.

steps.question: Eight element pairs are added by a vector unit with 4 lanes. How many add cycles does it need, and what is the speed-up over scalar?

reveal.text: Four elements per cycle: 8 ÷ 4 = **2 cycles**, against 8 for a scalar unit: a speed-up of **4**.

steps.result: With 8 lanes it would be 1 cycle.

steps.title: Vector registers and applications

items: A **vector register** holds many elements; a vector instruction like `vadd v1, v2, v3` adds them element by element
Classic vector supercomputers had registers of 64 elements; modern SIMD uses 128 to 512 bits
Only code with **independent, regular** operations on arrays benefits (data-level parallelism)
Typical applications: graphics, video and audio, image processing, machine learning, scientific simulation

blocks.text: Not everything vectorizes: loops with dependences between iterations or irregular branches stay scalar. Amdahl's Law applies again: a program with 80% vectorizable work and 8 lanes speeds up 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.8 ÷ 8) = 3.33 times.

steps.why: Vector hardware is the cheapest way to gain performance on data-parallel code.
steps.real: Libraries such as BLAS and image filters are hand-optimized with SIMD instructions.

mistake.wrong: Vector hardware speeds up every program.
mistake.right: Only the vectorizable fraction speeds up; the rest is limited by Amdahl's Law.

steps.title: Calculate: partial vectorization
steps.why: 80% vectorizable with 8 lanes: 3.33 times. With 4 lanes: 2.5 times. The limit is 5 times, however wide the vector unit.

steps.question: SIMD stands for:
steps.why: One instruction operates on multiple data elements.

steps.statement: A vector unit with 4 lanes always runs every program 4 times faster.
steps.why: Only the vectorizable part speeds up, and only if it divides evenly.

steps.title: The RISC principles

items: **Simple instructions** that take about one cycle each
**Fixed instruction length** (typically 32 bits): easy fetch and decode
**Load/store architecture**: only loads and stores touch memory; arithmetic works on registers
**Many registers** (32 or more)
Designed for **pipelining** (Classes 12 to 16)

blocks.text: These follow the four design principles of the course: simplicity favours regularity, smaller is faster, make the common case fast, good design demands good compromises.

steps.why: Simple, regular instructions make pipelines fast and compilers effective.
steps.real: All modern high-performance RISC designs (ARM, RISC-V) follow these ideas.

head: MIPS
RISC-V

steps.why: The three look very similar: they share the same RISC ideas, so skills from this course carry over directly.

mistake.wrong: MIPS, RISC-V and ARM are completely different designs.

steps.title: From the 8086 to x86-64

head: Year (about)
Processor
Milestone
rows: 16-bit; 8 general registers; the origin of the architecture

steps.why: Backward compatibility is the reason for x86's success and also for its complexity: each generation added features without removing the old ones.
steps.real: A program written for the 1980s PC can often still run on a modern x86 machine.

explainAgain.beginner: A city that kept all its old streets and kept adding new ones: everything still works but the map is complicated.

steps.title: Why x86 is called CISC

items: **Variable instruction length**: 1 to 15 bytes
**Two-operand** form (destination is also a source): `add eax, ebx`
Arithmetic can use a **memory operand**: `add eax, [rbx+8]` loads and adds in one instruction
Many **addressing modes** and special-purpose registers
Instructions that do a lot: string operations, complex calls

right.title: x86 (CISC): one instruction
items: `add eax, [rbx+8]`
Loads and adds in one go

steps.why: CISC code is compact, but variable length and complex instructions make decoding hard.
steps.real: Compactness mattered when memory was scarce; now decoding cost matters more.

steps.title: How a modern x86 core works inside

nodes.label: Decode
nodes.note: Complex instructions become one or more simple internal operations.

nodes.label: Out-of-order core
nodes.note: Register renaming, reservation stations, branch prediction and speculation execute the micro-ops.

steps.why: Modern x86 processors hide the CISC instruction set behind a RISC-like engine, so the ideas of this whole course apply inside them.
steps.real: This is why x86 can compete with RISC designs in performance, at a cost in complexity and power.

deeper.text: The decoder, the micro-op cache and the long pipeline are large parts of an x86 core's area and power.

steps.question: Which feature makes x86 a CISC instruction set?
options: Variable-length instructions and memory operands in arithmetic instructions
Only loads and stores access memory
steps.why: CISC trades simple regular instructions for powerful complicated ones.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why did x86 survive for decades although RISC designs were technically cleaner?
steps.answer: Software compatibility: a huge installed base of programs ran only on x86, so each new generation kept the old instructions. Intel and AMD also found a way to get RISC-like performance inside the chip by translating x86 instructions into micro-operations, which removed most of the performance disadvantage.

steps.title: Calculate: AMAT

blocks.title: Average memory access time

steps.why: 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 2.0 cycles. The same formula applies to every level of the hierarchy.

steps.title: Putting it together
steps.prompt: Put the path of a data load in order when the data is in the L1 cache but its translation is not in the TLB.
items: The CPU issues a virtual address
The TLB misses and the page table is read
The physical address is formed
The L1 cache is looked up with the physical address and hits
The data returns to the CPU
steps.why: Translation comes before the cache lookup in this simple model.

questions.q: Name one RISC principle and one CISC feature of x86.
questions.a: RISC: fixed-length simple instructions (or load/store). x86: variable-length instructions with memory operands.

questions.q: What limits the speed-up from SIMD or from extra cores?
questions.a: The fraction that cannot be vectorized or parallelized (Amdahl's Law).

questions.q: Which idea unites caches, the TLB and disk caches?
questions.a: Locality: recently and nearby used data is reused.

steps.question: Name the idea behind SIMD in one sentence.
steps.answer: One instruction applies the same operation to many data elements at once.

steps.question: State three RISC principles.
steps.answer: Simple fixed-length instructions; load/store architecture; many registers (and design for pipelining).
steps.solution: These make decoding easy and pipelines fast.

steps.question: Give two reasons x86 is called CISC and one way a modern x86 core hides it.
steps.answer: Variable-length instructions (1 to 15 bytes) and arithmetic instructions with memory operands; the core decodes them into simple micro-operations executed by a RISC-like engine.
steps.solution: CISC complexity is confined to the decoder.

steps.question: A program executes 2 billion instructions at CPI 1.5 on a 3 GHz clock. Then 40% of the execution time is made 10 times faster. Find the original time and the overall speed-up.
steps.mistake: Applying the 10× to the whole program.
steps.title: Exam practice: CPU equation

steps.question: Encode `add $t2, $s0, $s1` in hex. Convert 5.75 to IEEE 754 single precision (hex).
steps.solution: add: op 0, rs = $s0 = 16, rt = $s1 = 17, rd = $t2 = 10, shamt 0, funct 32. 5.75 = 101.11₂ = 1.0111 × 2²: exponent 129, fraction 0111…
steps.mistake: Putting rd first in the machine word.
steps.title: Exam practice: encoding and arithmetic

steps.question: 20 independent instructions run on a 5-stage pipeline. How many cycles, what is the speed-up over 5 cycles per instruction, and why is it below 5?
steps.answer: 24 cycles; speed-up 100 ÷ 24 = 4.17; below 5 because of the 4 fill cycles.
steps.solution: Pipelined time is n + k − 1 = 24. Non-pipelined time is 20 × 5 = 100.
steps.title: Exam practice: pipelining

steps.question: A 1 KiB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses: how many tag, index and offset bits? With hit time 1, miss rate 5% and penalty 20 cycles, what is the AMAT?
steps.solution: Lines = 64 (6 index bits); offset 4; tag 32 − 10 = 22. AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 2.0.
steps.mistake: Using the hit rate instead of the miss rate.
steps.title: Exam practice: caches and AMAT

steps.question: 4 KiB pages. Split virtual address 0x3A7C into page number and offset. If page 3 is in frame 5, what is the physical address?

steps.question: (a) MTTF 1,000 h and MTTR 1 h: availability? (b) Six 2 TB disks in RAID 5: usable capacity? (c) A program is 90% parallel: speed-up on 8 cores?
steps.mistake: Using RAID 5 capacity of all six disks.
steps.title: Exam practice: storage and parallelism

steps.question: Explain how RISC ideas and CISC compatibility meet inside a modern x86 processor, and name two techniques from this course that it uses.
steps.answer: The x86 instruction set stays CISC for compatibility, but the decoder translates instructions into simple micro-operations that execute on a RISC-like core. That core uses techniques from this course such as deep pipelining, out-of-order execution with register renaming, branch prediction and speculation, caches and SIMD.
steps.solution: A strong answer mentions micro-operations and at least two techniques.
steps.mistake: Saying x86 processors are not pipelined.
steps.title: Exam practice: synthesis
What you should remember
remember: SIMD applies one instruction to many data elements; the gain is limited by the vectorizable fraction (Amdahl's Law).
RISC: simple fixed-length instructions, load/store, many registers, pipelining-friendly; MIPS, RISC-V and ARM are close relatives.
x86 grew from the 8086 (1978) to x86-64 with full compatibility: variable-length CISC instructions, translated into micro-operations inside.
Performance: CPU time = IC × CPI ÷ clock rate; Amdahl's Law limits every improvement.
Processor: single-cycle, multi-cycle, pipelining, hazards, ILP, out-of-order, branch prediction.
Memory: locality, caches (tag/index/offset, AMAT), virtual memory and the TLB; storage and RAID; multicore with coherence, locks and Amdahl.

mistakes.wrong: Vector hardware speeds up every program.
RISC and CISC are unrelated to modern chips.
mistakes.right: x86 translates CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-operations.

mistakes.wrong: Each topic of the course stands alone.
mistakes.right: They connect: locality, Amdahl's Law and parallelism recur everywhere.
CPU time depends on instruction count, CPI and clock rate.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Vector and SIMD instructions exploit data parallelism but are limited by Amdahl's Law. RISC architectures such as MIPS, RISC-V and ARM share simple, regular design, while x86 kept CISC compatibility and uses micro-operations inside a RISC-like core. The course connects performance equations, instruction sets, datapath and pipelining, memory hierarchy, storage and multiprocessors through common ideas: locality, parallelism and Amdahl's Law.
